Fuel for Petrol Engines
Petrol is a common liquid fuel used for two and four-wheeler light passenger vehicles. It is a mixture of about 150 volatile hydrocarbons with carbon atoms between 4 to 12 per molecule. Petrol contains straight and branched-chain alkanes (paraffins), cyclic alkanes (naphthenes), unsaturated hydrocarbons with one double bond (olefins) and aromatic hydrocarbons, with an average chemical composition of C8.26H15.5.
This problem will explore combustion of petrol and related fuels being used commercially in petrol engines. Some useful data:

| Compound | Density (g cm–3) | ΔH°combustion (kJ mol–1) |
|---|---|---|
| n-octane (l) | 0.70 | ‒ 5470.3 |
| cyclohexane (l) | 0.77 | ‒ 3918.6 |
| isooctane (l) | 0.69 | ‒ 5461.0 |
| ethanol (l) | 0.79 | ‒ 1366.8 |

PART A: Combustion in Petrol Engines
The combustion of petrol can be understood with octane as a model fuel.
1.1 Draw structures of all possible stereoisomer(s) of octane having two chiral centers, in the wedge-dash representation.

The combustion of fuel starts with a homolytic cleavage of a C–H bond in a hydrocarbon, forming alkyl radicals. These radicals can undergo rearrangement to form more stable radicals. If the radicals generated are unstable even after rearrangement, the fuel can burn at low temperatures. Among the alkyl radicals generated by the octane isomers during combustion, those formed by isooctane (2,2,4-trimethylpentane) are most stable, some of which are stabilized by rearrangement.
1.2. Draw the structure(s) of all probable alkyl radical(s) that are formed from isooctane including those after rearrangement. Identify the most stable free radical by circling its structure.

In a petrol engine under certain conditions, some components of the fuel-air mixture forming less-stable free radicals may self-ignite without ignition by the primary flame front as shown in the diagram below. Such secondary flames outside the primary flame front create secondary heat and pressure waves. Multiple pressure waves in the cylinder can create shock waves and cause jerky movements of the piston. The shock waves also create a characteristic "pinging" sound, known as knocking. Knocking tendency of a fuel (causing jerky movements in vehicle) is quantified by octane number. The fuel that causes less knocking is considered better and is assigned a higher octane number.

[Diagram description: Two side-by-side diagrams of a petrol engine cylinder. The left diagram, labeled "Smooth combustion", shows a spark plug igniting the fuel mixture, creating a single, smooth "Primary Flame" front that expands downwards towards the piston. The right diagram, labeled "Knocking", shows a similar cylinder where the spark plug ignites a "Primary Flame", but a "Secondary flame front" has spontaneously ignited at the side of the cylinder, separate from the primary flame, creating multiple flame fronts.]

1.3. Arrange the following hydrocarbons in ascending order of their knocking tendency.
methylcyclohexane, isooctane, n-octane, toluene (methylbenzene)

1.4. Estimate the stoichiometric amount of air (in g) required for the complete combustion of 100 cm3 of a liquid fuel mixture containing n-octane and cyclohexane [70:30, v/v assuming volumes are additive]. Write balanced equations for the combustion of each component. Assume composition of air (v/v) at NTP as: Argon (0.95%), Nitrogen (78.08%) & Oxygen (20.95%).

Air-fuel ratio (λ) is the relative stoichiometric ratio between the mass of air and the mass of fuel that are injected in the engine. When λ = 1, the combustion mixture in the engine contains a stoichiometric amount of air and fuel; values of λ < 1 signify fuel-rich mixtures, while λ > 1 correspond to air-rich mixtures. This ratio affects the composition of emitted gases from the engine.

Concentration values of two gases in a petrol engine exhaust as a function of λ are presented as two curves in the graph here.
[Graph description: A line graph showing "Exhaust gas emissions (ppm)" on the y-axis versus "λ" on the x-axis. The x-axis ranges from 0.70 to 1.20. The y-axis ranges from 0.0 to 400.0. There are two unlabeled curves. Curve 1 starts at approximately 250 ppm at λ = 0.72, and steadily decreases as λ increases, reaching approximately 120 ppm at λ = 1.18. Curve 2 starts at approximately 40 ppm at λ = 0.72, increases to a peak of approximately 360 ppm around λ = 1.10, and then decreases to approximately 290 ppm at λ = 1.18.]

1.5. If 20% excess air (λ = 1.2) is injected in a petrol engine for combustion of a fuel mixture containing octane (85% v/v), cyclohexane (5% v/v), 2-butene (5% v/v) and toluene (5% v/v), identify the gases emitted in the exhaust in significant concentrations (above 200 ppm). Mark X for the correct option(s).
a) CO2
b) CO
c) Ar
d) NOx
e) N2
f) O2
g) unburnt hydrocarbons (HC)

PART B: Mixing Ethanol with Isooctane
Most governments have been imposing vehicle emissions regulations that are continually being tightened further. BS VI emission standards notified by the Government of India limit values of exhaust gases for two wheelers fitted with spark ignition engines as follows: CO (500 mg km–1), HC (100 mg km–1), NOx (90 mg km–1).
[Reference: The Emission Standards for Bharat Stage VI (BS-VI), Ministry of Road Transport and Highways, May 2020].

Changing fuel compositions can address some of the emission concerns. Ethanol is one of the alternative transportation fuels which is available as a byproduct from agricultural sources.

1.6. Consider the liquid fuel for an engine is changed from isooctane (F0) to a mixture containing 80% isooctane and 20% ethanol (v/v, assuming volumes are additive), known as F20.
(i) Estimate the difference in calorific values of these two fuels, C (F20) – C (F0), heat released per g.
(ii) By what percent CO2 emission is reduced on changing the fuel from F0 to F20 for the same distance covered by the vehicle? Assume 100% efficient combustion and the efficiency of engines in the two cases to be identical.

PART C: Ethanol Blended Petrol
Ethanol blended petrol in different proportions is being used in different parts of the world including India. E85 is blend of 85% ethanol and 15% petrol, E20 is 20% ethanol blended with 80% petrol and so on. The ignition temperature of fuel is the temperature at which it spontaneously ignites in atmospheric air without an external source of ignition. Certain facts associated with ethanol blended fuels are:
F1. Ethanol forms an azeotrope with water.
F2. Addition of double bonds to alkyl chain of a fuel mixture stabilizes some of its alkyl radicals.
F3. Ethanol molecules are inherently rich in oxygen.
F4. The ignition temperature of ethanol is 365 °C and that of petrol is 247 - 280 °C.
F5. Ethanol-blended petrol absorbs water from atmosphere.
F6. Oxygen containing fuels inhibit formation of soot.
F7. Latent heat of evaporation of ethanol is much higher than that of octanes.

1.7. State which of the following statements are correct/ incorrect for petrol engines and write the fact/s (F1 - F7) which justify your answer.
S1. The E20 blended fuel will exhibit lower knocking than E0.
S2. Temperature of air fuel mixture in an engine at the start of combustion would be lower for E85 than for E20.
S3. E85 fuel can be more damaging to the engine parts having metallic surfaces than E20.
S4. E85 fuel will result in more emissions of unburnt HC than E20 fuel, at λ = 1.
S5. Emission of particulate matter is significantly increased with E85.

Here is the step-by-step reasoning and the final answers for each part of the problem.

---

### PART A: Combustion in Petrol Engines

#### 1.1 Stereoisomers of octane with two chiral centers
The only isomer of octane ($C_8H_{18}$) with exactly two chiral centers is **3,4-dimethylhexane**. The chiral centers are at carbon-3 and carbon-4. Since the molecule is symmetric, it has three stereoisomers: a pair of enantiomers and one meso compound.

* **(3R, 4R)-3,4-dimethylhexane**: Both methyl groups are on wedges (or both on dashes).
* **(3S, 4S)-3,4-dimethylhexane**: Both methyl groups are on dashes (or both on wedges, representing the enantiomer).
* **(3R, 4S)-3,4-dimethylhexane (meso)**: One methyl group is on a wedge and the other is on a dash.

---

#### 1.2 Alkyl radicals from isooctane (2,2,4-trimethylpentane)
Isooctane has the structure: $(CH_3)_3\text{C}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)_2$. 

The primary radicals formed directly by homolytic cleavage of C–H bonds are:
1. **Primary radical (at C1/C1'/C1'')**: $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}(\text{CH}_2^\bullet)-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)_2$
2. **Secondary radical (at C3)**: $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}-\text{CH}^\bullet-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)_2$
3. **Tertiary radical (at C4)**: $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}-\text{CH}_2-\text{C}^\bullet(\text{CH}_3)_2$
4. **Primary radical (at C5/C4')**: $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)(\text{CH}_2^\bullet)$

**Rearrangements:**
* The secondary radical (2) can undergo a 1,2-hydride shift to form the tertiary radical (3), or a 1,2-methyl shift to form $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}^\bullet-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)_2$.
* The primary radical (4) can undergo a 1,2-hydride shift to form the tertiary radical (3).
* The primary radical (1) can undergo a 1,2-methyl shift to form $(\text{CH}_3)(\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3)\text{C}^\bullet-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)_2$.

**Most Stable Radical:**
The most stable free radical is the tertiary radical formed directly at C4:
$$\mathbf{(CH_3)_3C-CH_2-C^\bullet(CH_3)_2}$$
This radical is tertiary and stabilized by 8 $\alpha$-hydrogens (hyperconjugation).

---

#### 1.3 Knocking tendency order
The knocking tendency of a fuel is inversely proportional to its octane number (ON).
* **Toluene**: $\text{ON} \approx 120$ (lowest knocking tendency)
* **Isooctane**: $\text{ON} = 100$
* **Methylcyclohexane**: $\text{ON} \approx 75$
* **n-Octane**: $\text{ON} \approx -20$ (highest knocking tendency)

**Ascending order of knocking tendency:**
$$\text{toluene} < \text{isooctane} < \text{methylcyclohexane} < \text{n-octane}$$

---

#### 1.4 Stoichiometric amount of air for 100 cm³ of fuel mixture
* **Balanced Equations:**
  * **n-octane**: $\text{C}_8\text{H}_{18} (l) + 12.5 \text{O}_2 (g) \rightarrow 8 \text{CO}_2 (g) + 9 \text{H}_2\text{O} (l)$
  * **cyclohexane**: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12} (l) + 9 \text{O}_2 (g) \rightarrow 6 \text{CO}_2 (g) + 6 \text{H}_2\text{O} (l)$

* **Mass of components in 100 cm³ of fuel (70:30 v/v):**
  * Mass of n-octane = $70\text{ cm}^3 \times 0.70\text{ g cm}^{-3} = 49.0\text{ g}$
  * Mass of cyclohexane = $30\text{ cm}^3 \times 0.77\text{ g cm}^{-3} = 23.1\text{ g}$

* **Moles of components:**
  * Moles of n-octane = $\frac{49.0\text{ g}}{114.23\text{ g mol}^{-1}} = 0.4290\text{ mol}$
  * Moles of cyclohexane = $\frac{23.1\text{ g}}{84.16\text{ g mol}^{-1}} = 0.2745\text{ mol}$

* **Oxygen required:**
  * $\text{O}_2$ for n-octane = $0.4290 \times 12.5 = 5.3625\text{ mol}$
  * $\text{O}_2$ for cyclohexane = $0.2745 \times 9 = 2.4705\text{ mol}$
  * Total $\text{O}_2$ required = $5.3625 + 2.4705 = 7.833\text{ mol}$

* **Air required:**
  * Mole fraction of $\text{O}_2$ in air = $0.2095$
  * Total moles of air = $\frac{7.833\text{ mol}}{0.2095} = 37.39\text{ mol}$
  * Average molar mass of air ($M_{\text{air}}$):
    $$M_{\text{air}} = (0.0095 \times 39.95) + (0.7808 \times 28.01) + (0.2095 \times 32.00) = 28.95\text{ g mol}^{-1}$$
  * Mass of air = $37.39\text{ mol} \times 28.95\text{ g mol}^{-1} = \mathbf{1082.4\text{ g}}$ (or $\approx \mathbf{1083\text{ g}}$)

---

#### 1.5 Exhaust gases above 200 ppm at $\lambda = 1.2$
At $\lambda = 1.2$ (lean mixture with 20% excess air), complete combustion occurs. The major components of the exhaust gas are nitrogen, carbon dioxide, excess oxygen, argon, and nitrogen oxides ($\text{NO}_x$, which peaks near $\lambda = 1.1$ and remains around 290 ppm at $\lambda = 1.2$). Carbon monoxide ($\text{CO}$) and unburnt hydrocarbons ($\text{HC}$) are extremely low ($< 100\text{ ppm}$).

**Correct Options:**
* **a) CO2 [X]**
* **c) Ar [X]**
* **d) NOx [X]**
* **e) N2 [X]**
* **f) O2 [X]**

---

### PART B: Mixing Ethanol with Isooctane

#### 1.6 (i) Difference in calorific values: $C(F20) - C(F0)$
* **Calorific value of F0 (pure isooctane):**
  $$C(F0) = \frac{5461.0\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}}{114.23\text{ g mol}^{-1}} = 47.807\text{ kJ g}^{-1}$$

* **Calorific value of F20 (80% isooctane, 20% ethanol v/v):**
  In 100 cm³ of F20:
  * Mass of isooctane = $80 \times 0.69 = 55.2\text{ g}$
  * Mass of ethanol = $20 \times 0.79 = 15.8\text{ g}$
  * Total mass = $71.0\text{ g}$
  * Heat from isooctane = $\frac{55.2\text{ g}}{114.23\text{ g mol}^{-1}} \times 5461.0\text{ kJ mol}^{-1} = 2638.91\text{ kJ}$
  * Heat from ethanol = $\frac{15.8\text{ g}}{46.07\text{ g mol}^{-1}} \times 1366.8\text{ kJ mol}^{-1} = 468.76\text{ kJ}$
  * Total heat = $3107.67\text{ kJ}$
  * $C(F20) = \frac{3107.67\text{ kJ}}{71.0\text{ g}} = 43.770\text{ kJ g}^{-1}$

* **Difference:**
  $$C(F20) - C(F0) = 43.770 - 47.807 = \mathbf{-4.037\text{ kJ g}^{-1}}$$ (or $\approx \mathbf{-4.04\text{ kJ g}^{-1}}$)

#### 1.6 (ii) Percent reduction in $\text{CO}_2$ emission
For the same distance covered (same energy $Q$):
* **$\text{CO}_2$ from F0:**
  $$n_{\text{CO}_2}(F0) = \frac{Q}{47.80705} \times \frac{8}{114.23} = 0.00146493 \times Q\text{ mol}$$
* **$\text{CO}_2$ from F20:**
  $$n_{\text{CO}_2}(F20) = \frac{Q}{3107.67} \times \left[8 \times \left(\frac{55.2}{114.23}\right) + 2 \times \left(\frac{15.8}{46.07}\right)\right] = 0.00146468 \times Q\text{ mol}$$
* **Percent reduction:**
  $$\text{Reduction} = \frac{0.00146493 - 0.00146468}{0.00146493} \times 100\% = \mathbf{0.017\%}$$ (or $\approx \mathbf{0.02\%}$)

---

### PART C: Ethanol Blended Petrol

#### 1.7 Evaluation of statements S1 - S5
* **S1. The E20 blended fuel will exhibit lower knocking than E0.**
  * **Answer:** **Correct**
  * **Justification:** **F4** (The higher ignition temperature of ethanol compared to petrol reduces the tendency of the fuel to auto-ignite, thereby reducing knocking).

* **S2. Temperature of air fuel mixture in an engine at the start of combustion would be lower for E85 than for E20.**
  * **Answer:** **Correct**
  * **Justification:** **F7** (The much higher latent heat of evaporation of ethanol compared to octanes causes significant cooling of the air-fuel mixture as the fuel evaporates).

* **S3. E85 fuel can be more damaging to the engine parts having metallic surfaces than E20.**
  * **Answer:** **Correct**
  * **Justification:** **F5** (Ethanol-blended petrol absorbs water from the atmosphere, and the absorbed water can cause corrosion and damage to metallic engine parts).

* **S4. E85 fuel will result in more emissions of unburnt HC than E20 fuel, at $\lambda = 1$.**
  * **Answer:** **Correct**
  * **Justification:** **F4, F7** (The high latent heat of evaporation (F7) cools the mixture, and the high ignition temperature (F4) makes it harder to burn completely, especially near the cooler cylinder walls, leading to increased unburnt HC emissions).

* **S5. Emission of particulate matter is significantly increased with E85.**
  * **Answer:** **Incorrect**
  * **Justification:** **F6** (Oxygen-containing fuels like ethanol inhibit the formation of soot, so particulate matter emissions are significantly decreased, not increased).

This released public chemistry benchmark item is a conceptual polymer-recycling question. Do not give operational procedures; give final conceptual answers only.

PET has repeating unit [-O-C(=O)-C6H4-C(=O)-O-CH2-CH2-]n.

Part A. PET
2.1 A PET sample is heated with excess aqueous base, cleaving the ester bonds completely.
(i) Name or write the products.
(ii) From the resulting mixture, choose a sequence from the following processes to isolate the two monomers that can remake PET. For each chosen step, state the mixture being treated and the compound separated.
Processes: I filtration; II reduced-pressure distillation near 100 C; III extraction with toluene; IV treatment with aqueous sodium bicarbonate; V addition of water; VI treatment with iodine; VII acidification; VIII normal-pressure distillation near 100 C; IX heating under inert gas.

2.2 PET is treated with an unknown liquid B (3n equivalents) and a Lewis-acid-type acetate catalyst to give bis(2-hydroxyethyl) terephthalate, HO-CH2-CH2-O-C(=O)-C6H4-C(=O)-O-CH2-CH2-OH.
(i) Identify B.
(ii) Choose the catalyst role: (a) Lewis acid catalyst, (b) dehydrating agent, (c) acetylating reagent, (d) Bronsted base catalyst.
(iii) Classify the reaction: (a) elimination, (b) addition, (c) nucleophilic substitution/transesterification, (d) electrophilic substitution.

2.3 PET is treated with excess 2-aminoethanol and a zinc acetate catalyst. Give the products after complete reaction.

2.4 Which depolymerization route can obtain PET back with the least chemical waste/byproduct and least energy input: (a) water hydrolysis, (b) base hydrolysis, (c) treatment with B and the acetate catalyst, or (d) treatment with 2-aminoethanol and zinc acetate?

Part B. Polythene
Mechanical stress in air can introduce carbonyl-containing groups into some polyethylene chains. The original sheet is clear; the mechanically stressed sheet is cloudy/wrinkled.

2.5 Give generic species X, Y, and Z in an autoxidation scheme where oxygen reacts with a polymer radical to form a peroxy species and ultimately oxygen-containing chain products.

2.6 Choose the statements that can explain reduced transparency: (a) scattering from roughness/defects, (b) PET hydrolysis, (c) no chemical change is possible, (d) crystalline/defect domains scatter light.

2.7 Choose reasonable limitations for mechanical recycling: (a) lower purity worsens quality, (b) repeated processing can degrade chains, (c) it always returns pure monomer, (d) no sorting is needed.

2.8 Mark whether each limitation belongs to mechanical or chemical recycling: (a) sensitive to purity/degradation; (b) requires chemical reagents/separation; (c) product properties decline after repeated cycles.

Return concise numbered answers for all subparts.

   $$\text{CaO(s)} + \text{H}_2\text{O(l)} \rightarrow \text{Ca(OH)}_2\text{(aq)}$$

2. **Reaction of calcium hydroxide with carbon dioxide:**
   $$\text{Ca(OH)}_2\text{(aq)} + \text{CO}_2\text{(g)} \rightarrow \text{CaCO}_3\text{(s)} + \text{H}_2\text{O(l)}$$

---

### **3.2. Calculation of $K_c$**
* **Given:** 
  * $T = 835\ ^\circ\text{C} = 1108.15\text{ K}$
  * $P_{\text{CO}_2} = 0.236\text{ atm}$
  * $R = 0.08205\text{ L atm K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}$
* For the heterogeneous equilibrium: $\text{CaCO}_3\text{(s)} \rightleftharpoons \text{CaO(s)} + \text{CO}_2\text{(g)}$
  $$K_p = P_{\text{CO}_2} = 0.236\text{ atm}$$
* Using the relation $K_p = K_c(RT)^{\Delta n_g}$ (where $\Delta n_g = 1$):
  $$K_c = \frac{K_p}{RT} = \frac{0.236\text{ atm}}{(0.08205\text{ L atm K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1})(1108.15\text{ K})} \approx \mathbf{2.59 \times 10^{-3}\text{ mol L}^{-1}}$$

---

### **3.3. Thermodynamic Calculations**
First, calculate the standard enthalpy change ($\Delta H^\circ$) and standard entropy change ($\Delta S^\circ$) for Reaction 1:
$$\Delta H^\circ = \Delta H^\circ_f[\text{CaO(s)}] + \Delta H^\circ_f[\text{CO}_2\text{(g)}] - \Delta H^\circ_f[\text{CaCO}_3\text{(s)}]$$
$$\Delta H^\circ = (-635.6) + (-393.5) - (-1206.9) = +177.8\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$

$$\Delta S^\circ = S^\circ[\text{CaO(s)}] + S^\circ[\text{CO}_2\text{(g)}] - S^\circ[\text{CaCO}_3\text{(s)}]$$
$$\Delta S^\circ = 39.8 + 213.6 - 92.9 = +160.5\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1} = +0.1605\text{ kJ K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}$$

#### **(i) Standard free energy change ($\Delta G^\circ$)**
* **At $25\ ^\circ\text{C}$ ($298.15\text{ K}$):**
  $$\Delta G^\circ_{298} = \Delta H^\circ - T\Delta S^\circ = 177.8 - (298.15 \times 0.1605) = \mathbf{+130.0\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}}$$
* **At $850\ ^\circ\text{C}$ ($1123.15\text{ K}$):**
  $$\Delta G^\circ_{1123} = \Delta H^\circ - T\Delta S^\circ = 177.8 - (1123.15 \times 0.1605) = \mathbf{-2.5\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}}$$

#### **(ii) Threshold Temperature**
For $\text{CaCO}_3\text{(s)}$ to spontaneously decompose at $P_{\text{CO}_2} = 1\text{ atm}$, we require $\Delta G^\circ < 0$:

Here are the step-by-step reasoning and final answers for each part of the problem.

---

### **4.1. Structure of Maltose**
Maltose is a disaccharide formed from two units of D-glucopyranose joined by an $\alpha(1\rightarrow 4)$ glycosidic bond. 

* **Left Ring (Non-reducing end):** $\alpha$-D-glucopyranose
  * C1: $-\text{O}-$ glycosidic link pointing **down** (alpha)
  * C2: $-\text{OH}$ pointing **down**
  * C3: $-\text{OH}$ pointing **up**
  * C4: $-\text{OH}$ pointing **down**
  * C5: $-\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ pointing **up**
* **Right Ring (Reducing end):** D-glucopyranose (shown here as the $\alpha$-anomer)
  * C1: $-\text{OH}$ pointing **down** (for $\alpha$-maltose) or **up** (for $\beta$-maltose)
  * C2: $-\text{OH}$ pointing **down**
  * C3: $-\text{OH}$ pointing **up**
  * C4: Oxygen of the glycosidic bond from the left ring (pointing **down**)
  * C5: $-\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ pointing **up**

**Haworth Representation of $\alpha$-Maltose:**
```
       HO-CH2                  HO-CH2
         |                       |
       .-O-.                   .-O-.
      /     \  O-glycosidic   /     \
     |       |____ O ____    |       |-- OH (anomeric)
     |       |           \   |       |
      \     /             \ / \     /
       `---'               `---' 
```

---

### **4.2. Student 1 and Student 2 Analysis**

#### **a) Positive Tollen's Test Equation**
The reducing sugars (such as glucose) in the mixture reduce Tollen's reagent to metallic silver:
$$\text{CH}_2\text{OH}(\text{CHOH})_4\text{CHO} + 2[\text{Ag}(\text{NH}_3)_2]^+ + 3\text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{CH}_2\text{OH}(\text{CHOH})_4\text{COO}^- + 2\text{Ag(s)} + 4\text{NH}_3 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$$
* **Reactant (D-Glucose):** Cyclic hemiacetal in equilibrium with the open-chain aldehyde.
* **Product (D-Gluconate):** Carboxylate form of D-gluconic acid (open-chain with C1 as $-\text{COO}^-$).

#### **b) Step iv Reaction (Grey-Black Coloration)**
When dipped in $\text{AgNO}_3$ followed by $\text{NaOH}$, silver oxide ($\text{Ag}_2\text{O}$) precipitates as a brownish-black solid over the entire plate:
$$2\text{AgNO}_3\text{(aq)} + 2\text{NaOH}\text{(aq)} \rightarrow \text{Ag}_2\text{O(s)} + 2\text{NaNO}_3\text{(aq)} + \text{H}_2\text{O(l)}$$

#### **c) Step v Reaction (Disappearance of Background Color)**
Sodium thiosulfate dissolves the unreacted, insoluble silver oxide by forming a soluble silver-thiosulfate complex, clearing the background:
$$\text{Ag}_2\text{O(s)} + 4\text{Na}_2\text{S}_2\text{O}_3\text{(aq)} + \text{H}_2\text{O(l)} \rightarrow 2\text{Na}_3[\text{Ag}(\text{S}_2\text{O}_3)_2]\text{(aq)} + 2\text{NaOH}\text{(aq)}$$

#### **d) Spotting Reaction for Maltose**
Maltose (reducing sugar) selectively reduces the silver oxide on the spot to insoluble, black metallic silver:
$$\text{Maltose} + \text{Ag}_2\text{O} + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{Maltobionate}^- + 2\text{Ag(s)} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

#### **e) Identification of Spots**
* **Spot A:** Glucose
* **Spot D:** Glucose
* **Spot F:** Maltotriose

#### **f) TLC Spot Sequence & Positions**
* **Correct Option:** **(D)** lower mobility of larger carbohydrate molecules than smaller ones.

---

### **4.3. Student 3 Analysis (Phenol-Acid Method)**

#### **a) Structures of Y and Z**
* **Intermediate Y ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_6\text{O}_3$):** 5-Hydroxymethylfurfural (5-HMF)
  * *Structure:* A furan ring containing a $-\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ group at C5 and a $-\text{CHO}$ group at C2.
* **Compound Z ($\text{C}_{18}\text{H}_{14}\text{O}_4$):** A quinoid condensation dye product.
  * *Structure:* A central $sp^2$ carbon double-bonded to a cyclohexadienone ring ($=\text{C}_6\text{H}_4=\text{O}$) and single-bonded to a $p$-hydroxyphenyl group ($-\text{C}_6\text{H}_4\text{OH}$) and a 5-hydroxymethyl-2-furyl group ($-\text{C}_4\text{H}_2\text{O}-\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$).

#### **b) Reaction causing the decrease in $I(D):I(E)$**

#### **c) Intensity ratio of spots $I(F):I(B)$**

Iodine is a purple-black crystalline solid at room temperature that has a unique ability to sublime into a violet-purple vapour.

The mixture gave off purple vapour, which then formed shiny purplish-black crystals on the sides of the vessel. Courtois had discovered solid iodine!

Elemental iodine is not naturally found in its free state. It is found in seaweeds as iodide ($\text{I}^-$), and in caliche (saltpetre deposits) and associated groundwaters as iodate ($\text{IO}_3^-$).

The white solid that precipitates out is filtered, washed with water, dried, and finely ground. This purified white solid is then heated with potassium carbonate solution to give potassium iodide solution and a red-brown precipitate.
